summary:
Space Mission Design game is an interactive, browser-based 3D game that helps students design and operate a Lunar Ice Mapper mission. Players begin with a limited budget, purchase and assemble spacecraft components, choose a launch vehicle and launch site, and configure a lunar orbit. A connected educational model calculates spacecraft mass, delta-v, power demand, usable battery capacity, mission cost and science data return.
The game visualizes launch, staging, lunar transfer, orbital operations and data transmission. Design choices produce meaningful consequences, including loss of power or control, encouraging students to diagnose problems and improve their missions.
To connect engineering decisions with real science, the project uses NASA LRO/LROC south-pole illumination data, NASA visualization assets and published planetary parameters. It clearly separates observed data from simulated observations and simplified flight scenarios.
The project addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning mission planning into an accessible, repeatable learning experience. It helps students understand engineering trade-offs, interpret scientific evidence and learn from unsuccessful designs.
details:
Project overview

Space Mission Design Game is an interactive, browser-based 3D educational game built around a Lunar Ice Mapper mission. It turns space mission design into a practical learning experience: students receive an objective, work within a limited budget, purchase components, assemble a spacecraft, select a launch vehicle and launch site, and configure a lunar orbit. They then operate the mission, examine its outcome and improve their design.

How it works

The application connects spacecraft configuration to engineering calculations and visible mission behavior. It calculates dry and wet mass, propellant requirements, available delta-v using the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, lunar orbital speed and period, electrical demand, solar generation, usable battery capacity, storage, communication capacity and mission cost. Students can adjust orbital altitude and inclination and compare the consequences for operations and simulated science return.

A 3D flight view shows launch, staging, transfer toward the Moon, spacecraft separation, solar-panel deployment, lunar operations and data transmission. Camera controls, automatic playback, pause, replay and speed settings let students follow the mission. Launch and transfer animations use simplified educational scenarios rather than real flight telemetry. Engineering consequences are connected to the design and operational decisions: insufficient energy can exhaust the battery, inadequate propulsion can prevent the planned maneuver, and communication choices can limit the amount of data returned. A debrief and exportable mission report help students explain the outcome and revise the spacecraft.

NASA data and scientific grounding

The science explorer uses genuine NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter/Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera south-pole illumination data. Source references, metadata and units help students investigate how illumination relates to a polar mission. NASA visualization resources provide Earth and Moon imagery, while published planetary parameters support the educational orbital calculations. Observed illumination, simulated sensor coverage and simulated science return are clearly distinguished. Illumination data are not measurements of water-ice abundance, and the game does not claim to discover or verify lunar ice.

Benefits and intended impact

The project is intended for students, educators and people exploring aerospace engineering for the first time. It makes the relationships between mass, propulsion, power, cost, orbit and communications easier to understand through interaction. Students can compare configurations, learn from unsuccessful missions and repeat experiments without physical hardware or launch expenses. The intended impact is to strengthen systems thinking, scientific data literacy and evidence-based engineering decisions. The game provides a setting for classroom discussion and independent exploration; educational outcomes have not yet been established through a formal learning study.

Tools, languages and software

The application is developed primarily in TypeScript, with React for the interface and Three.js with React Three Fiber for interactive 3D graphics. HTML and CSS with Tailwind CSS provide page structure and styling. Zustand manages application state, Zod validates structured inputs, and Recharts displays engineering results. Vite and Node.js support development and production builds. Vitest, React Testing Library and Playwright support automated verification; ESLint and Prettier support code quality. Git and GitHub support version control and collaboration, and OpenAI Codex assisted development. The game runs in a web browser on a conventional computer; it requires no specialized aerospace hardware.

Creativity and design considerations

The creative contribution is the connection between a spacecraft shopping and assembly experience, transparent engineering calculations, NASA science exploration and a continuous 3D mission narrative. Instead of ending at a design score, the game lets students observe consequences and explain why their mission succeeded or failed. The team considered accessibility, browser performance, reproducible behavior, budget constraints, scientific attribution and the balance between realism and usability. Flight scenarios, component specifications, costs and failure thresholds include educational assumptions. The project is a learning tool, not a mission-grade trajectory predictor or a certified spacecraft design system.
